subject: biology

items.q: Which line shows the equation for photosynthesis written in chemical symbols?
items.correct: CO2 and H2O react to form C6H12O6 and O2.
items.misconception: C6H12O6 and O2 react to form CO2 and H2O.
items.why: The two equations look like mirror images of each other, so reactants and products get swapped. Being told that plants 'give out oxygen' is also heard as 'plants do not use oxygen', and the site of each reaction is mixed up. Photosynthesis is represented by: carbon dioxide + water → (light) glucose + oxygen, and it takes place in the chloroplasts. The glucose produced in photosynthesis may be used for respiration, so plants carry out both reactions.
items.random_wrong: CO2 and O2 react to form C6H12O6 and H2O.

items.q: Which statement describes photosynthesis as an endothermic reaction?
items.correct: Energy is transferred from the environment to the chloroplasts.
items.misconception: Energy is transferred from the chloroplasts to the surroundings.
items.why: Students meet glucose as the energy store used in respiration, so they assume that any reaction which produces glucose must release energy. The word 'light' written over the arrow is also read as a product of the reaction rather than as the energy that is taken in. Photosynthesis is an endothermic reaction: energy is transferred from the environment to the chloroplasts by light. Energy is taken in by the reaction, it is not given out.
items.random_wrong: Energy is transferred from the surroundings to the mitochondria.

items.q: A student measures the rate of photosynthesis of pondweed by counting bubbles of oxygen. She counts 90 bubbles in 3 minutes. What is the rate of photosynthesis?
items.why: Students record the largest number in their results table and read it as 'how much photosynthesis happened'. Rate is not yet treated as a quantity measured per unit of time, so the time column is ignored or is multiplied in rather than divided by. Rate of photosynthesis is calculated as the amount of product formed divided by the time taken, for example bubbles of oxygen per minute or cm3 of oxygen per minute.

items.q: A student plots the rate of photosynthesis of pondweed against light intensity at a constant temperature. The graph rises steeply and then becomes a horizontal line. Which statement explains the horizontal part of the graph?
items.correct: Another factor, such as temperature, is now limiting the rate.
items.misconception: Light intensity is still limiting the rate on the flat part.
items.why: Light is taught as the thing that drives photosynthesis, so students treat it as the only factor that matters and look for damage to the plant or a fault in the experiment to explain a flat line, instead of using the idea of a limiting factor. Light intensity affects the rate of photosynthesis, but the factors interact and any one of them may be the factor that limits photosynthesis. Where the graph is flat, a factor other than light intensity is limiting the rate.
items.random_wrong: The plant has switched from photosynthesis to respiration.

items.q: A graph shows the rate of photosynthesis against light intensity at 20 °C and at 30 °C, both at the same carbon dioxide concentration. Both curves rise and then become horizontal, but the 30 °C curve becomes horizontal at a higher rate. Which statement about the graph is correct?
items.correct: Temperature is limiting the rate where the 20 °C curve is flat.
items.misconception: Light intensity is limiting the rate where the 20 °C curve is flat.
items.why: Light is taught as the thing that drives photosynthesis, so students treat it as the only factor that matters and look for damage to the plant or a fault in the experiment to explain a flat line, instead of using the idea of a limiting factor. Light intensity affects the rate of photosynthesis, but the factors interact and any one of them may be the factor that limits photosynthesis. Where the graph is flat, a factor other than light intensity is limiting the rate.
items.random_wrong: Temperature is limiting the rate on the steep part of each curve.

items.q: A lamp is moved from 10 cm to 20 cm from a piece of pondweed. Light intensity is inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the lamp. What happens to the light intensity reaching the pondweed?
items.correct: It falls to 1/4 of the intensity at 10 cm.
items.misconception: It falls to 1/2 of the intensity at 10 cm.
items.why: Inverse proportion is normally met as y being proportional to 1/x, so students apply simple inverse proportion to the distance and do not square it. Distances in centimetres are also used directly in the fraction instead of the change in distance. Light intensity is inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the light source. Doubling the distance reduces the light intensity to 1/2 squared, which is one quarter.
items.random_wrong: It falls to 1/16 of the intensity at 10 cm.

items.q: How does a plant obtain the amino acids it uses for protein synthesis?
items.correct: Amino acids are made from glucose and nitrate ions.
items.misconception: Amino acids are made from starch and nitrate ions.
items.why: The iodine test for starch is used in class to show that a leaf has photosynthesised, so students conclude that starch is the direct product of the reaction and stop distinguishing it from the glucose in the equation. The equation shows that photosynthesis produces glucose (C6H12O6). The glucose produced may then be used for respiration, converted into insoluble starch for storage, used to produce fat or oil for storage, used to produce cellulose, or used to produce amino acids.
items.random_wrong: Amino acids are absorbed from the soil by the roots.

items.q: Does raising the temperature always increase the rate of photosynthesis?
items.correct: Raising the temperature increases the rate only while temperature is the limiting factor; at high temperatures the enzymes controlling photosynthesis are denatured and the rate falls.
items.misconception: The warmer a plant is kept, the faster it photosynthesises, so raising the temperature increases the rate whatever the starting temperature is.
items.why: Students generalise from the rising part of a rate-temperature graph, and from the rule met in chemistry that heating makes reactions go faster. They forget that photosynthesis is controlled by enzymes, which are denatured at high temperatures. Temperature affects the rate of photosynthesis. It increases the rate while it is the limiting factor, but above the optimum temperature the enzymes are denatured and the rate falls.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Where do the proteins in a plant come from?
items.correct: The plant makes them: glucose produced in photosynthesis is used with nitrate ions absorbed from the soil to produce amino acids for protein synthesis.
items.misconception: Plants take in ready-made protein from the soil through their roots, which is why fertiliser has to be added to the soil.
items.why: Fertiliser is described as 'plant food', so students picture the soil as supplying finished food substances such as protein, rather than ions that the plant uses to build molecules for itself. To produce proteins, plants use nitrate ions that are absorbed from the soil. These are used with the glucose produced in photosynthesis to produce amino acids for protein synthesis.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
